subject: computer-science

moments.title: FORTRAN released
moments.body: After three years of work, IBM releases FORTRAN (Formula Translation) for the IBM 704. Backus's team had to convince sceptical engineers that a compiler could produce machine code as efficient as hand-written assembly. They largely succeeded — and the productivity gain was overwhelming.
moments.takeaway: The first major high-level language proved that programmers did not need to think in machine code. Productivity rather than efficiency drove the abstraction.

moments.title: COBOL designed
moments.body: Hopper, a US Navy commander and PhD mathematician, had built FLOW-MATIC (1955), the first English-like programming language. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) builds on it. Hopper's insight: business code should read like English so non-programmers could verify what it did.

quote.text: It's easier to ask forgiveness than it is to get permission.

moments.takeaway: Hopper's COBOL became the language of business computing for sixty years. An estimated 200+ billion lines of COBOL are still running in 2024 — mostly in banks, insurance and government.

now.title: Languages today
now.body: FORTRAN remains in scientific high-performance computing (climate models, computational fluid dynamics). COBOL runs ~70% of global business transaction volume by some estimates. Hopper is buried with full military honours at Arlington; the USS Hopper destroyer is named for her.
now.open_questions: How long will COBOL persist? US state unemployment systems collapsed during COVID-19 partly because COBOL maintainers had retired.

reflection: Hopper also coined 'debugging' after finding an actual moth in a relay of the Harvard Mark II (1947). The log entry — with the moth taped in — is preserved at the Smithsonian.
